Main.sentence: Thomas Richard Carper (born January 23, 1947) is an American politician and former military officer who served from 2001 to 2025 as a ___E:United States senator U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate)___ from ___E:Delaware U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware)___ .

A member of the ___E:Democratic Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States))___ , Carper served from 1983 to 1993 in the ___E:United States House of Representatives U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives)___ and from 1993 to 2001 as the 71st ___E:governor of Delaware U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_governors_of_Delaware)___ .

A native of ___E:Beckley, West Virginia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beckley,_West_Virginia)___ , Carper graduated from ___E:Ohio State University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_State_University)___ on an ___E:NROTC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NROTC)___ scholarship.

Serving as a ___E:naval flight officer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_flight_officer)___ in the ___E:U.S. Navy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Navy)___ from 1968 until 1973, he flew the ___E:P-3 Orion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-3_Orion)___ as a tactical coordinator and mission commander  and saw active duty in the ___E:Vietnam War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War)___ .

After leaving the active duty Navy, he remained in the ___E:U.S. Naval Reserve U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Naval_Reserve)___ for another 18 years and eventually retired with the rank of ___E:Captain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_(United_States))___ (O-6).

Upon receiving his ___E:MBA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Business_Administration)___ from the ___E:University of Delaware U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Delaware)___ in 1975, Carper went to work for the state of Delaware in its economic development office.
He was elected state treasurer, serving from 1977 to 1983 and leading the development of Delaware's first cash management system.
Encouraged by local politicians, Carper successfully ran for Delaware's only seat in the U.S.
House of Representatives in 1982. He served five terms in the House, where he chaired the Subcommittee on Economic Stabilization.
In 1992, he swapped positions with term-limited Republican Governor ___E:Mike Castle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Castle)___ , and the two were easily elected to each other's seats.

Carper governed for two terms as a moderate, business-oriented ___E:New Democrat U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Democrats_(United_States))___ , following the lead of the two previous Republican governors.
Carper was elected to the U.S.

Senate in ___E:2000 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_United_States_Senate_election_in_Delaware)___ , defeating Republican incumbent ___E:William Roth U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Roth)___ .

He was reelected by landslides in ___E:2006 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_United_States_Senate_election_in_Delaware)___ , ___E:2012 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_United_States_Senate_election_in_Delaware)___ , and ___E:2018 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_United_States_Senate_election_in_Delaware)___ .

He served as one of four deputy Democratic whips, the chairman of the ___E:Senate Environment and Public Works Committee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Environment_and_Public_Works)___ and on the ___E:Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Homeland_Security_and_Governmental_Affairs)___ and the ___E:Finance Committee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Finance)___ .
Carper was the senior senator in ___E:Delaware's congressional delegation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_congressional_delegations_from_Delaware)___ and the dean of the delegation.
He was the last Vietnam War veteran to serve in the Senate.
Carper was born in Beckley, West Virginia, the son of Mary Jean (née Patton) and Wallace Richard Carper.

He grew up in ___E:Danville, Virginia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danville,_Virginia)___ , and graduated from ___E:Whetstone High School U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whetstone_High_School_(Columbus,_Ohio))___ in ___E:Columbus, Ohio U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus,_Ohio)___ .

He then graduated from the ___E:Ohio State University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_State_University)___ in 1968, where he was a midshipman in the ___E:Naval ROTC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_ROTC)___ and earned a ___E:Bachelor of Arts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts)___ degree in ___E:economics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics)___ .
At Ohio State, Carper became a member of the Beta Phi Chapter of the ___E:Delta Tau Delta U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_Tau_Delta)___ fraternity.

Carper earned an ___E:MBA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Business_Administration)___ from the ___E:University of Delaware U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Delaware)___ in 1975.

Serving as a ___E:Naval Flight Officer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Flight_Officer)___ in the ___E:U.S. Navy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Navy)___ from 1968 until 1973, he served three tours of duty in ___E:Southeast Asia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia)___ during the Vietnam War. He remained in the ___E:U.S. Naval Reserve U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Naval_Reserve)___ as a ___E:P-3 aircraft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_P-3_Orion)___ mission commander for another 18 years and retired with the rank of ___E:Captain (O-6) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_(United_States_O-6))___ .
While in college at the Ohio State University, Carper worked on the presidential campaign of U.S.
Senator ___E:Eugene McCarthy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_McCarthy)___ .

In Delaware, he worked as the campaign treasurer for University of Delaware professor James R. Soles in his unsuccessful 1974 bid for the ___E:U.S. House of Representatives U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._House_of_Representatives)___ .
After receiving his MBA degree in 1975, Carper went to work for the State of Delaware's economic development office.
In 1976, after developing good relationships with members of the state party leadership, he took out a $5,000 personal loan to fund his campaign to be Treasurer of Delaware.
In the election, he defeated the favored Republican Party candidate, Theodore Jones.
He served three terms, from January 18, 1977, through January 3, 1983, during which time he oversaw the development of Delaware's first cash management system.
Senator ___E:Joe Biden U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden)___ and other prominent Democrats convinced Carper to run for Delaware's only seat in the U.S.
House of Representatives.

Incumbent Republican ___E:Thomas B. Evans Jr. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_B._Evans_Jr.)___ sought reelection, and although he had been caught in a compromising "association" on a golfing trip with the lobbyist Paula Parkinson, was still considered a strong candidate.

Carper was considered well-positioned until three weeks before Election Day, when the New York Post published an article claiming that the "dirtiest campaign in the country is being waged in tiny Delaware", which suggested that Carper had abused his wife and stepchildren.
But when rumors spread that the story was "planted" by a supporter of Evans, Carper bounced back, with public opinion seeming to be that the allegations inappropriately exploited private issue.
Carper and his wife both denied the allegations in 1982, but he later admitted to having slapped her. Carper defeated Evans.
Carper served five terms in the House.
He won his second term in 1984, defeating Elise R. W. du Pont, the wife of retiring Governor ___E:Pete du Pont U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_du_Pont)___ .

He then easily defeated Republicans Thomas S. Neuberger in 1986, James P. Krapf in 1988 and Ralph O. Williams in 1990. He was a member of the ___E:U.S. House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._House_Committee_on_Financial_Services)___ and the ___E:U.S. House Committee on Merchant Marine and Fisheries U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._House_Committee_on_Transportation_and_Infrastructure)___ .
He chaired the House Subcommittee on Economic Stabilization.
In these positions, he worked to allow banks into the securities business and to discourage the dumping of sludge into the ocean.

During his years in the House, Carper sought to gain better control of Delaware's Democratic Party organization in hopes of someday becoming governor, focusing on heavily Democratic and populous ___E:New Castle County U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Castle_County,_Delaware)___ .

Its Democratic organization was controlled by Eugene T. Reed, a former ironworker and longtime party boss who was then among several politicians in both parties implicated in illegal money raising practices.

To address this corruption and rescue the Democratic Party's reputation, Carper recruited Joseph E. Reardon, a ___E:DuPont Company U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DuPont_Company)___ chemist, as a candidate for New Castle County Democratic Party chairman.
By early 1989, Reardon had been elected, replacing Reed at the head of a newly reformed party organization.
In 1990, Carper defeated a Reed ally, Daniel D. Rappa, in the Democratic primary for U.S. representative.

Republican Governor Michael Castle was ___E:term-limited U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Term_limit)___ and unable to seek reelection in 1992. The result was what became known as "the Swap", with Castle seeking Carper's seat in the U.S.
House of Representatives and Carper seeking the governorship.
Neither faced substantive opposition for either post.
Carper defeated Republican B. Gary Scott and was elected governor.
He served two terms.
Carper positioned himself as a moderate, business-oriented governor, emphasizing economic development and business recruitment.

This included the prevention of the closure of the ___E:General Motors U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Motors)___ automobile operation near ___E:Newport, Delaware U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport,_Delaware)___ , and convincing pharmaceutical giant ___E:AstraZeneca U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AstraZeneca)___ to construct its new headquarters in the state.

Carper led an ongoing effort to reduce ___E:income tax U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Income_tax_in_the_United_States)___ rates, eliminate the ___E:marriage penalty U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage_penalty)___ and ___E:estate tax U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estate_tax)___ , cut the public ___E:utility tax U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Utility_tax&action=edit&redlink=1)___ , and eliminate the ___E:gross receipts tax U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_receipts_tax)___ for many small businesses.
Delaware's credit rating improved from among the worst in the nation to AAA. Carper also retained Castle's standards-based education programs.
Other programs included a fully funded ___E:Head Start program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_Start_(program))___ and a prescription-drug benefit for seniors.
Carper had high approval ratings, but was criticized by some old-line Democrats and union leaders.

As a tribute to Anne Marie Fahey, who had been a youth ___E:mentor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mentorship)___ before her death, then-Governor Carper also became a mentor, and began actively promoting mentoring programs throughout Delaware's business community.
As a result, by the end of his last term, Delaware held the highest per-capita ratio of youth mentors in the country.
Carper also established the Delaware Mentoring Council to help sustain this legacy.
Due to term limits, Carper had to retire as governor in 2000, and sought election to the U.S.

Senate against incumbent Republican ___E:William Roth U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Roth)___ , declaring his candidacy in September 1999.  Some had concerns about Roth's age of 79, compared to Carper's relative youth.
Roth started the campaign with a 2-to-1 spending advantage, but Carper went into the final month with more than $1 million on hand.  He defeated Roth, 56% to 44%.

Roth received more votes than Republican presidential candidate ___E:George W. Bush U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush)___ , suggesting that the strength of the Democratic turnout for the presidential election was key in Carper's victory. [citation needed] Some commentators attributed Roth's defeat to his age and health, as he collapsed twice during the campaign, once during a television interview and once during a campaign event.

Carper sought reelection in 2006. He was unopposed in the Democratic primary and faced Republican nominee ___E:Jan C. Ting U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_C._Ting)___ , a professor of law who had narrowly beaten airline pilot Michael D. Protack in the Republican primary.
Carper was easily reelected, 67% to 27%.
As the 2012 election cycle began, a ___E:Super PAC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_action_committee)___ was created to oppose Carper's reelection campaign.

The Hill quoted ___E:Patrick Davis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Davis_(politics))___ , the custodian of records and agent for Renew Delaware as saying, "Tom Carper has served in the United States Senate for a long time and has been part of the downturn in our economy." Delaware Politics noted that the election would be costly for the Republican candidate and that Carper was heavily favored to win a third term.  A Carper spokesperson, Emily Spain, was quoted in The Hill saying that Carper was successful in his previous campaigns "because he works hard, takes nothing for granted, and puts the needs and interests of Delaware first."  Carper won the Democratic primary with 88% of the vote and faced off against the only Republican candidate who filed for the race, businessman ___E:Kevin Wade U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_L._Wade)___ .
He was reelected with 66% of the vote.

In 2018, Carper sought his fourth Senate term.   His campaign contributors included ___E:DuPont U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DuPont)___ , his third-largest contributor since 2013. Between 2013 and 2018, he received $2.1 million from ___E:political action committees U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_action_committees)___ .

In the Democratic primary, Carper was challenged from the left by Kerri Evelyn Harris, a ___E:US Air Force U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force)___ Veteran, who, unlike Carper, supports a ___E:single-payer healthcare U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-payer_healthcare)___ .
Carper won the primary with roughly 65% of the vote.  It was his most competitive primary in recent history.
In the general election, Carper defeated Republican nominee Rob Arlett, 60.0% to 37.8%.
On May 22, 2023, Carper announced that he would not seek reelection in 2024. In his press conference, Carper endorsed U.S.
Representative ___E:Lisa Blunt Rochester U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisa_Blunt_Rochester)___ .
Senator Carper retired from the United States Senate on January 3, 2025. He was the last remaining combat veteran of the Vietnam War serving in the U.S.
Senate.

Carper served with the Democratic minority in the ___E:108th U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/108th_United_States_Congress)___ and ___E:109th U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/109th_United_States_Congress)___ Congresses and was part of the Democratic majority in the ___E:110th U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/110th_United_States_Congress)___ Congress.
At the beginning of the ___E:107th U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/107th_United_States_Congress)___ Congress, the Democratic Party was in the minority, but later held the majority.
Carper was a member of the moderate ___E:Democratic Leadership Council U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Leadership_Council)___ (DLC), of which he served as vice chair.
In 2004, Carper became part of the Senate Democratic leadership.

As a member of a four-person "Executive Committee", he is one of four deputy whips. ___E:David Broder U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Broder)___ of The Washington Post has called Carper "a notably effective and non-partisan leader, admired and trusted on both sides of the aisle."

During the ___E:January 6 United States Capitol attack U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_6_United_States_Capitol_attack)___ , Carper said he did not support invoking the ___E:Twenty-fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twenty-fifth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution)___ or ___E:impeachment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_impeachment_in_the_United_States)___ of Trump.
But hours later, he called on Trump to resign.
He also called the attackers "domestic terrorists".
That evening, he voted to certify the ___E:2021 United States Electoral College vote count U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_United_States_Electoral_College_vote_count)___ .
Carper's committee assignments for the 118th Congress are as follows:
Carper is considered a ___E:moderate Democrat U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Democrats_(United_States))___ .
He has a 13% conservative rating from the ___E:American Conservative Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Conservative_Union)___ .

Carper voted for the ___E:Budget Control Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budget_Control_Act_of_2011)___ , against cut, cap and balance, for debt increase, for debt ceiling increase, for ___E:debt limit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debt_limit)___ increase, for the stimulus, for TARP, for the ___E:Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patient_Protection_and_Affordable_Care_Act)___ , for ___E:SCHIP U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children%27s_Health_Insurance_Program)___ , for DREAM, and for the Immigration Reform Act of 2006.
Carper has a mixed record on ___E:abortion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion)___ issues.
In 2003, he was one of 17 Democrats who broke with the majority of their party by voting to ban ___E:partial-birth abortion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial-birth_abortion)___ .
He also voted against banning abortion after 20 weeks of pregnancy, but voted to ban the use of federal funds for abortion.
In 2018, he opposed President Trump's proposal to defund ___E:Planned Parenthood U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_Parenthood)___ .

Carper was given a 50% rating by ___E:NARAL Pro-Choice America U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NARAL_Pro-Choice_America)___ , indicating a mixed record on abortion, according to their scoring, and a 25% rating from the ___E:anti-abortion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-abortion)___ ___E:National Right to Life Committee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Right_to_Life_Committee)___ .

After ___E:Roe v. Wade was overturned U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dobbs_v._Jackson_Women%27s_Health_Organization)___ in June 2022, he said the decision was "unconscionably cruel and wrong" and that it was a "dark day for our country and our Constitution."

In April 2019, Carper was one of thirty-four senators to sign a letter to President ___E:Donald Trump U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump)___ encouraging him "to listen to members of your own Administration and reverse a decision that will damage our national security and aggravate conditions inside Central America", asserting that Trump had "consistently expressed a flawed understanding of U.S. foreign assistance" since becoming president and that he was "personally undermining efforts to promote U.S. national security and economic prosperity" through preventing the use of Fiscal Year 2018 national security funding.
The senators argued that foreign assistance to Central American countries created less migration to the U.S., citing the funding's helping to improve conditions in those countries.

In January 2024, Carper voted against a resolution, proposed by ___E:Bernie Sanders U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Sanders)___ , to apply the ___E:human rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_violations_against_Palestinians_by_Israel)___ provisions of the ___E:Foreign Assistance Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Assistance_Act)___ to ___E:U.S. aid to Israel's military U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_support_for_Israel_in_the_Gaza_war)___ .

The proposal was defeated, 72 to 11.  In March 2024, Carper led a letter to the Biden administration urging the U.S. to recognize a "nonmilitarized" ___E:Palestinian state U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_Palestine)___ after the war in Gaza.  This letter was signed by 19 Democratic senators who support a two-state solution to the ___E:Israeli-Palestine conflict U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_conflict)___ .
Carper joined 23 other Senate Democrats in signing a letter supporting Obama taking executive action to reduce gun violence.
In 2013, he voted to ban high-capacity magazines of over 10 bullets.
In 2016, Carper participated in the ___E:Chris Murphy gun control filibuster U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Murphy_gun_control_filibuster)___ .

In response to the ___E:2017 Las Vegas shooting U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Las_Vegas_shooting)___ , Carper called for more gun laws, specifically background checks and mental health screenings.

In January 2019, Carper was one of forty senators to introduce the Background Check Expansion Act, a bill that would require background checks for either the sale or transfer of all firearms including all unlicensed sellers.

Exceptions to the bill's background check requirement included transfers between members of law enforcement, loaning firearms for either hunting or sporting events on a temporary basis, providing firearms as gifts to members of one's immediate family, firearms being transferred as part of an inheritance, or giving a firearm to another person temporarily for immediate self-defense.

He joined in the unsuccessful attempt to tie the ___E:Bush tax cuts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bush_tax_cuts)___ to ___E:deficit reduction U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_budget_deficit)___ and has supported additional funding for ___E:school choice U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_choice)___ programs and ___E:charter schools U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charter_schools)___ .
He has also sought additional funding for railroad projects and for rail security.

He strongly supported legislation to limit ___E:class action lawsuits U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_action_lawsuits)___ and to restrict ___E:personal bankruptcy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_bankruptcy)___ .
In addition, he is a strong proponent of ___E:free trade U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_trade)___ .
In 2012, Carper sponsored a bill, eventually passed and signed into law, that required government agencies to identify $125 billion in expected waste and fraud.

Carper and ___E:George Voinovich U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Voinovich)___ of ___E:Ohio U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio)___ proposed a 25-cent raise in the federal gasoline tax; 10 cents would go to pay down the debt and the rest toward improving the nation's infrastructure.
The measure was proposed in November 2010.  The measure did not pass.

On May 14, 2011, The Wall Street Journal criticized a postal-bailout bill co-sponsored by Carper and ___E:Susan Collins U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Collins_(politician))___ (R- ___E:Maine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine)___ ).
The bill would give $50–$75 billion to ___E:USPS U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Postal_Service)___ , and would underwrite pension obligations for retired postal workers.
The bailout would cost three times the savings of the 2011 federal budget.

On August 1, 2019, the Senate passed a bipartisan budget deal that raised spending over current levels by $320 billion and lifted the debt ceiling for the following two years in addition to forming a course for funding the government without the perceived fiscal brinkmanship of recent years.

Carper joined ___E:Joe Manchin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Manchin)___ and Republicans ___E:Mitt Romney U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitt_Romney)___ and ___E:Rick Scott U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Scott)___ in issuing a statement asserting that "as former Governors, we were responsible for setting a budget each year that was fiscally responsible to fund our priorities.
That's why today, we, as U.S.
Senators, cannot bring ourselves to vote for this budget deal that does not put our country on a fiscally sustainable path."

Carper proposed the creation of a ___E:National Park U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park)___ in Delaware, the Coastal Heritage Park, in four locations along the ___E:Delaware River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_River)___ and ___E:Delaware Bay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_Bay)___ .

In January 2009, Carper briefly chaired a ___E:Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Environment_and_Public_Works)___ hearing on the ___E:Tennessee Valley Authority's coal ash spill U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Fossil_Plant_coal_fly_ash_slurry_spill)___ in ___E:Kingston, Tennessee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston,_Tennessee)___ .
However, he did vote for ___E:Keystone XL Pipeline U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keystone_XL_Pipeline)___ , but has since expressed disappointment in that vote.

Carper supports the ___E:EPA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EPA)___ and ___E:Clean Air Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clean_Air_Act_(United_States))___ and blames states to the west of Delaware for its air pollution, calling them "America's tailpipe".

In April 2019, Carper was one of forty-one senators to sign a bipartisan letter to the housing subcommittee praising the ___E:Housing and Urban Development Department U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Housing_and_Urban_Development)___ 's Section 4 Capacity Building program as authorizing "HUD to partner with national nonprofit community development organizations to provide education, training, and financial support to local community development corporations (CDCs) across the country" and expressing disappointment that President Trump's budget "has slated this program for elimination after decades of successful economic and community development." The senators wrote of their hope that the subcommittee would support continued funding for Section 4 in Fiscal Year 2020.

Carper co-wrote the "Protecting Cyberspace as a National Asset Act of 2010"  introduced on June 19, 2010, by Senator ___E:Joe Lieberman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Lieberman)___ (Senator Susan Collins is the third co-author of this bill).

If signed into law, this controversial bill, which the American media dubbed the " Kill switch bill ", would grant the ___E:President U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States)___ emergency powers over the Internet.
All three co-authors of the bill, however, issued a statement claiming that instead, the bill "[narrowed] existing broad Presidential authority to take over telecommunications networks".

Carper was quoted as saying that the bill "would create a National Center for Cybersecurity and Communications in the ___E:Department of Homeland Security U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Homeland_Security)___ , with a Senate-confirmed director to oversee security of the federal government's computer networks.

The center would also identify vulnerabilities and help secure key private networks – like utilities and communications systems – that, if attacked or commandeered by a foreign power or cyberterrorists, could result in the crippling of our economy."
In May 2010, Carper introduced an amendment to limit state regulators from enforcing consumer regulations on national banks and their subsidiaries.

It would also remove a Senate legislative measure requiring the ___E:Office of the Comptroller of the Currency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_the_Comptroller_of_the_Currency)___ to find a "substantive standard" on regulation, before the office could move to preempt.
The ___E:White House U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House)___ opposed Carper's amendment.
The amendment passed by a vote of 80–18.

On September 21, 2011, The Wall Street Journal noted that President ___E:Barack Obama U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama)___ 's job-creation plans were drawing resistance from Senate Democrats.

The article quoted Carper as saying, "I think the best jobs bill that can be passed is a comprehensive long-term deficit-reduction plan. That's better than everything else the president is talking about combined."
In April 2014, the United States Senate debated the ___E:Minimum Wage Fairness Act (S. 1737; 113th Congress) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_Wage_Fairness_Act_(S._1737;_113th_Congress))___ .
